summary: Discusses issues in deploying IPv6 in mobile networks, where smartphones and other mobile devices accelerate IPv4 address exhaustion. It is a reference for service providers and network designers and replaced RFC 6312.

plainLanguage.summary: Phones are using up the old Internet addresses fast, so the newer kind of address is needed. This guide explains to phone companies what that switch means in practice: where to put the address translation, what happens when a phone roams into a country whose network has not switched yet, and which parts of the network can be shared with fixed broadband.

questions: where to place nat in a mobile network
subtitle: What phone operators have to think about when they move their networks from IPv4 to IPv6.

tldr.problem: Mobile Internet growth is using up IPv4 addresses, and mobile networks have quirks (gateways, roaming, billing) that make IPv6 deployment harder than in fixed networks.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC walks through address exhaustion, where to put NAT (centralized, distributed or hybrid), IPv6-only deployment with roaming and VoLTE, and fixed-mobile convergence, using existing solutions. It proposes no new protocols.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational reference for operators and network designers. It obsoletes RFC 6312, which carried the wrong RFC number in its header; the specification is otherwise unchanged.

facts.label: Security section
facts.value: States that no new vulnerabilities are introduced

sections.title: Introduction: Why Mobile Networks Are Different
sections.content:
The dramatic growth of the Mobile Internet is accelerating the exhaustion of the available IPv4 addresses. It is widely accepted that IPv6 is necessary for the continued operation and growth of the Internet in general and of the Mobile Internet in particular. While IPv6 brings many benefits, certain unique challenges arise when deploying it in mobile networks, and this document describes such challenges and outlines the applicability of the existing IPv6 deployment solutions. It is therefore a useful reference for service providers as well as network designers, and it proposes no new protocols and suggests no new protocol specification work.

The primary considerations addressed are the exhaustion of public and private IPv4 addresses and its implications for mobile network deployment architecture, the placement of Network Address Translation functionality and its implications, IPv6-only deployment considerations with their roaming implications, and Fixed-Mobile Convergence and its implications for the overall architecture.

For the most part the document assumes the 3GPP 3G and 4G network architectures, though the considerations are general enough for other mobile network architectures as well. The RFC Editor note records that the document obsoletes RFC 6312 because of a publishing error that put the wrong RFC number in that document's header, and that the specification is otherwise unchanged.
sections.plainLanguage: There is no shortage of advice about moving to IPv6. This document looks at the parts that mobile networks add: phone numbers of a sort, roaming between operators, and billing that has to follow each subscriber.

sections.title: The Reference Architecture and Its Vocabulary
sections.content:
The document gives a reference architecture for a mobile network. A Mobile Node connects to the mobile network either through its Home Network or through a Visited Network when the user is roaming outside the Home Network. In the 3GPP architecture the Mobile Node accesses the network by connecting to an Access Point Name, which maps to a mobile gateway. Roughly speaking, an APN is similar to a Service Set Identifier in a wireless LAN: it is a logical concept that specifies what kinds of services, such as Internet access or video streaming, a Mobile Node is entitled to, and each APN can specify what type of IP connectivity, meaning IPv4, IPv6 or both, is enabled on it.

While an APN directs a Mobile Node to an appropriate gateway, the node needs an end-to-end link to that gateway. In LTE networks this link is realised through an Evolved Packet System bearer, and in 3G UMTS networks through a Packet Data Protocol context. That link traverses several nodes. The Base Station provides the wireless connectivity. The Access Network Gateway forwards IP packets to and from the Mobile Node; it is typically not the node's default router and does not perform IP address allocation, and it sits either in the Home Network or in the Visited Network. The Mobile Network Gateway is the default router and provides IP address management; it offers Quality of Service, applies subscriber-specific policy and enables billing and accounting, operations sometimes called subscriber management, and it is typically in the Home Network. The Border Router borders the Internet for the mobile network and does not perform subscriber management.

Two further functions complete the picture. Authentication, Authorization and Accounting is used for subscriber authentication and authorization for services as well as for generating billing and accounting information, and in 3GPP environments it is provided through the Home Location Register or Home Subscriber Server functionality. The Policy and Charging Rule Function enables the application of policy and charging rules at the Mobile Network Gateway.
sections.plainLanguage: A phone's traffic passes through several boxes. The base station is the radio mast, the access gateway hands packets to and from the phone, the mobile gateway is the one that assigns addresses and does the billing, and the border router joins the mobile network to the rest of the Internet.

sections.title: IPv4 Address Exhaustion in a Mobile Network
sections.content:
It is generally agreed that the pool of public IPv4 addresses is nearing exhaustion. The IANA has exhausted the available slash-8 blocks for allocation to the Regional Internet Registries, and the registries themselves have either run out of their blocks or are projected to exhaust them in the near future. For providers there are two simultaneous approaches: delaying the exhaustion of the IPv4 address pool by conserving it, and introducing IPv6 in operational networks.

Delaying public exhaustion involves assigning private IPv4 addresses to end users, or extending an IPv4 address with the use of port ranges, which requires tunnelling and additional signalling. A mechanism such as the Network Address Translator is used at the provider premises rather than the customer premises to manage the private address assignment and access to the Internet. The document focuses on translation mechanisms such as NAT44, which translates between public and private IPv4, and NAT64, which translates between public IPv6 and public IPv4, because the 3GPP architecture already defines a tunnelling infrastructure with the GPRS Tunnelling Protocol and allows for dual-stack and IPv6-only deployments.

In a mobile network the IPv4 address for a Mobile Node is assigned by the Mobile Network Gateway, in conjunction with Packet Data Network connectivity establishment. There can be one or more such connections active at any time, each supporting both IPv4 and IPv6 traffic or only one of them, and the IPv4 address is assigned at establishment or afterwards with DHCP. To delay the exhaustion of public addresses, that address has to be a private address translated into a shared public address, so a private-public translation mechanism is needed in the mobile network.

LTE requires an always-on connection so that a mobile user can be reliably reached in an All-IP network, because Voice over IP in LTE has no circuit-based infrastructure. If that always-on connection used IPv4 addressing, a private address would be needed for every node that attaches, which could significantly affect the availability and usage of private addresses. One way out is to make the always-on connection IPv6 and establish the IPv4 connection only when the user needs it. The 3GPP standards also specify deferred IPv4 address allocation on a dual-stack connection, which has the advantage of a single connection for both protocols while deferring the IPv4 address until an application needs it, but this requires a dynamic configuration protocol such as DHCP and appropriate triggers, and such support does not exist today in mobile phones. In the existing 3G networks there is no requirement for an always-on connection, the pre-Release-8 deployments do not support the dual-stack connection, and so two separate connections are needed to carry IPv4 and IPv6 traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: Every phone that is always reachable needs an address of its own, and that is what runs out. The document suggests giving phones IPv6 addresses for the always-on connection and handing out an old-style address only when an application really needs one.

sections.title: Where to Put the NAT
sections.content:
NAT44 functionality is needed to conserve the available pool and delay public exhaustion, but the private pool itself is not abundant for large networks. The so-called NET10 block has approximately 16.7 million private IPv4 addresses starting with 10.0.0.0, and a large mobile service provider network can easily have more than 16.7 million subscribers attached at a given time, so the management of the private pool and the placement of NAT44 becomes important.

NAT placement matters for other reasons as well. Access networks generally need to produce network and service usage records for billing and accounting, and in mobile networks the subscriber management features, meaning Quality of Service, policy and billing, can be fairly detailed. Because a NAT introduces a binding between two addresses, those bindings become necessary information for subscriber management: the offered Quality of Service on a private address and on the shared public address may need to be correlated for accounting, and if the address seen by the provider's Application Servers is not unique, the Policy and Charging Rule Function has to inspect the NAT binding to tell subscribers apart. There may also be legal requirements for storing the NAT binding records. These problems disappear with the transition to IPv6.

Deployments vary in how they allocate address pools. The centralized model manages the pool at a common node, such as the border router, shared by several gateways, and it served well before 3G, but it now forces providers to address private pool exhaustion and scalable NAT. To tackle private exhaustion in the centralized model, the common NAT and each of the gateways would have to support overlapped private addresses, which means tunnelling mechanisms such as GRE, MPLS VPNs or IP-in-IP encapsulation to give each NAT session a unique identifier. Centralising the NAT conserves the private pool and lets the operator's enterprise network use IPv6 from the gateway to the border router, but it needs extra protocols to correlate NAT state with subscriber session information, gives suboptimal Mobile Node to Mobile Node communication, lacks a subscriber-aware NAT function, and means a failure of the NAT function affects every connected gateway.

In the distributed model the private address management and the NAT function both sit at the Mobile Network Gateway, so each gateway has a block of 16.7 million unique addresses, sufficient for the subscribers active on it. Distributing the NAT to the edge of the network lets each gateway reuse the available NET10 block, which avoids the problem of overlapped private addresses in the core. Since the gateway is where subscriber management lives, NAT state correlation is readily enabled, and it already has interfaces to the AAA and PCRF functions. It can also pass certain traffic through without translation to the Application Servers inside the provider's domain, so that those servers identify subscribers by unique private addresses. The disadvantage is the absence of centralised addressing and centralised management of NAT. A hybrid model puts the NAT in a dedicated device, which behaves like the distributed model when the pool supports unique addressing and like the centralized model when it does not, and in any case has to give the NAT session binding information to an external entity for correlation.
sections.plainLanguage: There are three places to put the box that rewrites addresses. The document compares them and finds that putting it at the mobile gateway, where the subscriber records already live, is the easiest to run, while a shared box at the edge saves the private address pool but needs extra bookkeeping.

sections.title: IPv6-Only Deployment and Roaming
sections.content:
NAT should be viewed as an interim solution until IPv6 is widely available for mobile users for all or most practical purposes. There are three dimensions to an IPv6-only deployment: the network, the mobile nodes and the applications, and the goal is to reach the coordinate IPv6, IPv6, IPv6 from IPv4, IPv4, IPv4. There are several paths. The classic dual-stack model traverses the coordinate where each dimension supports co-existence, which appears to be the path of least disruption, although it means supporting large-scale NAT and, in the existing 3G networks, the cost of separate packet data contexts. The other intermediate coordinate of interest is IPv6, IPv6, IPv4, where the network and the nodes are IPv6-only while the Internet applications are recognised to be predominantly IPv4, which ironically requires interworking between IPv6 and IPv4 so that the IPv6-only nodes can reach IPv4 services, meaning that in order to disengage NAT for IPv4 to IPv4 another form of NAT is introduced to speed up the adoption of IPv6.

For IPv6 to IPv4 translation there is no overlapping private address problem, because every IPv6 address is unique and there are plenty of them, so no protocol is needed to disambiguate NAT sessions. There is however an additional requirement for DNS64 functionality, which must ensure that the synthesised AAAA record correctly maps to the IPv6-to-IPv4 translator.

Both the network and the nodes need to be IPv6 capable. The 3GPP design for LTE already requires the network nodes and the mobile nodes to support IPv6, and although there are no requirements for the transport network to be IPv6, an operational IPv6 connectivity service can be deployed with existing tunnelling mechanisms in an IPv4-only transport network. A provider may therefore choose to enforce IPv6-only connections and address assignment for its own subscribers in its Home Network, which is feasible for newer nodes when the network can provide IPv6-only connectivity and IPv6 to IPv4 interworking for Internet access, while existing nodes still need IPv4-only connectivity.

Application migration brings its own challenges, since applications on the node also need to be IPv6-capable. Some IPv4-only applications may make use of alternative access such as WiFi, and a related challenge is the use of IPv4 literals in application layer protocols such as XMPP, or in content such as HTML or XML, because some applications expect their clients to supply IPv4 addresses as literals. Voice over LTE brings unique challenges of its own: the signalling for voice is generally expected to be available for free while the call itself is charged on its duration, a separation of signalling and payload that is unique to voice, and providers and users generally require voice service regardless of roaming.

Roaming is unique to mobile networks and introduces new challenges, because providers can control their own network design but not their peers' networks. A provider with an IPv6-only deployment has to support IPv4 addressing when its own subscribers roam to networks that do not offer IPv6, for instance when an IPv6-only LTE deployment roams onto a 3G network with no IPv6 connectivity, since a connection involves the base station, the access gateway and the mobile gateway. There are also inbound roamers to an IPv6-ready provider network whose nodes are not IPv6 capable, and that network has to support IPv4 connectivity for them. IPv6-only deployments should be encouraged alongside the dual-stack model, which is the recommended IETF approach, and they can be phased in for newer nodes while the existing ones continue to demand IPv4-only connectivity.

Fixed-Mobile Convergence is harder, because access networks are disparate. Roaming is not a consideration in fixed access networks, an All-IP mobile provider is required to provide voice service while a fixed provider is not, and a link in fixed networks generally carries both IPv6 and IPv4 traffic while not all mobile networks have links capable of that. The same mechanisms for delaying exhaustion and introducing IPv6 apply, but the exact solutions vary: tunnelling of private IPv4 packets within IPv6 is feasible in fixed networks where the endpoint is often a cable or DSL modem but not in mobile networks where the endpoint is the node itself, and encapsulation-based mechanisms such as 6rd are useful where a residential gateway can act as a tunnel endpoint. The document concludes that a provider's core network appears to be the place where most convergence is feasible.
sections.plainLanguage: Going all the way to IPv6 on the network is possible, but the phone may still meet old servers on the Internet, and the phone may still roam onto a network that has not switched. Both of those force the operator to keep the old addressing working for a while.

sections.title: Summary and Conclusion
sections.content:
The document summarises its discussion. On IPv4 address exhaustion, as providers begin to deploy IPv6, conserving the available IPv4 pool implies the need for network address translation in mobile networks, and at the same time providers can use the 3GPP constructs such as the APN and packet data connectivity to introduce IPv6 without affecting the predominantly IPv4 Internet access, so the IETF dual-stack model applies readily.

On the placement of NAT, both the centralized and distributed models have relative merits: by letting each Mobile Network Gateway manage its own NET10 pool, the distributed model reuses the available private pool and avoids the problems of non-unique private addresses without extra protocol mechanisms, and it augments the subscriber management functions at the gateway with easy correlation of NAT sessions with the rest of the subscriber session state. Existing deployments with centralised address management can continue their legacy architecture by placing the NAT at a common node, which also reuses the private pool but needs extra protocol extensions to tell overlapping addresses apart and to integrate with policy and billing infrastructure.

On IPv6-only deployments, the model is feasible in the LTE architecture for an operator's own services and applications, while existing nodes still expect IPv4 address assignment. Roaming requires a provider to support IPv4 connectivity when its outbound users roam into a network that is not IPv6-enabled, and similarly for inbound users whose nodes are not IPv6-capable, and IPv6-to-IPv4 interworking is necessary for IPv6-only nodes to reach the IPv4 Internet. On Fixed-Mobile Convergence, the examples show the differences between fixed and mobile requirements, and while some harmonization of functions may be possible across the access networks, the core network is perhaps better suited to a converged architecture. The security considerations section states that the document does not introduce any new security vulnerabilities.
sections.plainLanguage: The short version: keep the old addressing working through translation, share addresses where you must, put the translation where the subscriber records are, and move new phones to IPv6 first while the rest of the world catches up.

viz.caption: WHERE THE PARTS OF A MOBILE NETWORK SIT

layers.label: Mobile Node
layers.detail: The phone or device, reached through an APN

layers.label: Access Network Gateway
layers.detail: Forwards IP packets to and from the mobile node

layers.label: Mobile Network Gateway
layers.detail: The default router: assigns addresses, applies policy, enables billing

layers.label: Border Router
layers.detail: Borders the Internet for the mobile network

viz.caption: THE NETWORK ELEMENTS AND WHAT EACH ONE DOES

items.title: Base Station
items.text: Provides the wireless connectivity to the mobile node.

items.title: Access Network Gateway
items.text: Forwards IP packets to and from the mobile node. It is typically not the default router and does not allocate addresses.

items.title: Mobile Network Gateway
items.text: The default router. Provides address management, Quality of Service, subscriber policy, and billing and accounting.

items.title: Border Router
items.text: Borders the Internet for the mobile network, and does no subscriber management.

items.title: AAA
items.text: Authentication, Authorization and Accounting for subscribers and for billing information.

items.title: PCRF
items.text: Policy and Charging Rule Function: applies policy and charging rules at the mobile gateway.

viz.caption: THE THREE PLACES TO PUT THE ADDRESS TRANSLATION

cells: A common node, such as the border router, shared by several gateways
Keeps legacy deployments and reuses the private address pool
Needs extra protocols to tell overlapping addresses apart and to correlate NAT state with subscriber state
Each gateway manages 16.7 million addresses, so no overlap in the core, and the state sits with the subscriber records
No centralised address management or centralised NAT management
Behaves like either model depending on the address pool
Must supply the session binding information to another system for correlation
